title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Native-App Winners
dek: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on the ability to create from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to help you locate AI's current position, countering the 'this time is different' optimism, while also revealing the opportunity window for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants in transition.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three phases: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally native applications. The consensus on token as a unit of measure by 2026 signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called 'lobster') mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares this to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; those who can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may hold the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming states that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies is unlikely to be the big winners of the native application phase. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, and AOL was valued at $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies or refineries extracting base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars weren't built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will definitely emerge, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
points.body: Corporations correspond to the industrial-era bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial era, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but by 'what problem needs solving,' with both humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Therefore, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will die out. Future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's New Lab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, rather than command and assessment.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that 'being good is not the same as being excellent.' Being good is sustained growth with positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disagrees, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success. Thus, 'excellence is determined after the fact.' Those who are merely good easily fall into a cycle of self-validation, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, attribute success to the era and partners, and are mission-driven rather than valuation-driven. When identifying founders, he asks, 'What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?' If the answer is 'a ten-billion-dollar company,' that's mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a 'strategy generation system': organizations must build an environment and network where strategic insights emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial era. His methodology is 'look ten years, think three years, act one year,' with the core being 'think three years': you need to see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term vision. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, allowing the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The correct analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Two current paths—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to know in advance which will be faster. Historically, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford's assembly line in 1913 that scaling began; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and selling ten thousand robots is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the most unsafe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next; IBM and Microsoft are the only possible exceptions, and even they are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms are likely to be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. He therefore calls his mission 'being a happy researcher' and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system to shift from 'knowledge indoctrination' to 'open exploration,' because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate system, primarily composed of researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword referring to taking control of one's own destiny, actively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command.

quotes.text: The most successful companies are always contrarian, but being contrarian doesn't guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It might do well later, but it's highly likely not to be the big player, the big winner in the native application phase.
Companies in the first phase struggle to survive into the second, and companies in the second phase struggle to survive into the third.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future, there will be more interesting things. How many people today are happy going to work at a company? They're not.

My technology is so great, I've created so much value, why might my company not be worth much? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits. You're just a company that isn't worth much.

Excellence is determined after the fact, because you overcome negative feedback again and again. When everyone doesn't recognize you, you finally prove with enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I've always believed that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe. Whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
